Birds on a Wire

CountingLimits
Game: Birds land at random on a wire, and we run many trials to see how much of the wire the gaps to their closest neighbours cover on average.
How to play: Set the number of birds and trials, then press Go. Press Stop to pause, Repeat for more trials, or press Enter on the wire to add one trial at a time.
A wire with birds and highlighted gaps, and a plot of the average covered length against the number of birds.

Look for the math

Here is a question about chance on a line. Drop birds at random on a wire and look at the spaces between neighbouring birds. If you keep doing it, does the covered length settle down to a number you can predict? This is a geometric probability question, and the answer is surprisingly steady.

Which gaps get a highlight

Each bird looks at the two gaps beside it and claims the smaller one - the gap towards its closest neighbour. A gap is highlighted when at least one of its two birds claims it. That happens unless the gap is bigger than both of its neighbours: only such a local maximum is left unmarked. The two gaps at the very ends of the line are always marked, because there is no gap beyond them to compare with.

Two and three birds, checked exactly

With two birds there are only two end gaps, so the marked length is just the distance between them. With three birds there are again only end gaps, so the marked length is the span from the first bird to the last. The average span of two or three random points on a unit wire is 1/3 and 1/2. The logic test checks every possible ordering on a small grid, including equal gaps, and confirms both numbers.

Larger flocks: a steady constant

With a handful of birds the covered fraction sits near one half; as the flock grows it eases down. The untouched gaps are the local maxima, which tend to be the longer ones. In the long run the fraction approaches 7/18, about 0.389. One way to see it: for evenly spread random gaps the chance that a gap of length x beats both neighbours is (1 - e^-x)^2, and integrating x (1 - e^-x)^2 e^-x gives 11/18 of the wire left out, hence 7/18 covered. This is an expected value, and the law of large numbers is why the plotted average stops jumping around when trials are added. The logic test checks the simulated value against 7/18.

A small quirk in the original applet

The page says the applet runs "a specified number of trials for every number of birds between the specified minimum and maximum values". Almost: when it moves to the next bird count it draws that trial too, without the counter change the other trials get. So the first bird count runs the chosen number of trials and every later count runs one extra. The applet then divides by the chosen number when it shows the average. This harmless off-by-one is kept here, and the logic test records the true counts rather than hiding the quirk.

Try 2 to 2 birds first, then raise the maximum a little at a time and watch where the dots settle. Does the last average move much when you press Repeat?
